activities.title: A Drive in the Countryside
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the passage about a drive in Wales and answer the questions that follow.
activities.compensates: Teacher-led reading aloud and comprehension questions.

content.passage:
Last year, I spent my holiday in Wales, where the scenery is wonderful. One bright, sunny day, I decided to go for a drive. I drove out of town along the coast road. The sea was to my left about two kilometres away. Between the sea and the road was farmland. In one field there were a lot of cows with their heads down, grazing. In another field, close to me, a farmer on a tractor was ploughing. Behind the plough were lots of birds, looking for something to eat in the newly turned-over soil.

To the right of the road were some high, rocky hills. I turned off the main coast road and soon I was in a deep valley. Hills rose on both sides of the road. At first, the road climbed gently, but as I drove higher, it got steeper and steeper. Further up I could see a river to the left. I drove higher and higher and the river got narrower and narrower, until it was just a stream.

Near the top of the hill, the road ended. I got out of the car and climbed to the peak to look at the view of the valley below. At the end of the valley I could see the farmer on his tractor. Away in the distance I could just make out the sea. As I looked, I began to feel hungry and thirsty.

I went back down to the stream below. The water was cold and clear and tasted very good. I sat on a rock to eat my sandwiches, my back warmed by the sun. Suddenly a cloud came across the sun. I felt cold. A mist came down over the mountain. Soon I would not be able to see where I was going. I knew I had to leave. I put away a half-eaten sandwich, got into the car and drove back down the valley.

What happened to the river as the writer drove higher up the hill?

activities.instruction: Listen to the descriptions of two men. Look at the image and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the picture that best matches each description. This is based on Workbook page 3, Activity A.

questions.question: Listen to the first description. Which man is being described?
questions.explanation: The description mentions straight, greyish hair, a tired face, an old black jacket, and battered shoes, which best matches Man B.

questions.question: Now, listen to the second description. Which man is being described?
questions.explanation: The description mentions brightly polished, pointed shoes, a smart jacket, a pointed beard, glasses, and long dark hair, which best matches Man F.

content.transcript: It isn’t easy to describe the man. He could have been anyone. He had straight, greyish hair. It was thin and quite long in places. I don’t think he went to a hairdresser’s very often. Perhaps he thought it wasn’t worth it as he didn’t have much hair lift. His eyes were tired - the eyes of a man who has seen a lot of sadness or worry. His face was tired too - tired and covered in lines. It wasn’t an ugly face, just a very very old one. He wore an old black jacket - not a sports jacket but the jacket from a long forgotten suit. Under the jacket was an open-necked shirt. His trousers, which didn’t match the jacket and looked too big for him, were a dull blue colour and full of holes. On his feet were a pair of battered shoes - not much good in the rain. ### The first thing you noticed about the man was his shoes. They were brightly polished and an unusual shape - long and pointed. Most people were wearing heavy shoes or boots, which made his stand out. Above the shoes, he was wearing a pair of light coloured trousers which made quite a contrast with the dark shoes. His jacket was the same colour as the shoes, very smart and beautifully cut. He had a white shirt and a flower pattern tie. His face was long and thin, and his short, pointed beard made it look even longer. His glasses caught the light as he moved his head from side to side quickly, like a bird, and his long dark hair swung from side to side.

questions.question: Which sentence best describes the passenger's luggage?

content.transcript: Passenger: Excuse me! Excuse me, miss! Clerk: Can I help you, sir? Passenger: Yes. I've just got off the plane from Paris, but my luggage hasn't arrived yet. Clerk: Can you describe your luggage, sir? Passenger: What am I going to do? No clothes! Nothing! Clerk: Calm down, sir. There's no point in getting upset. Now, can you describe your luggage? Passenger: Two suitcases. Clerk: Are they the same size? Passenger: No. One is bigger than the other. Clerk: Are they the same colour? Passenger: Well, they're both green, but the smaller one is a very light green. Clerk: Ok. What shape are they? Passenger: The larger one is rectangular. The smaller one is more square-looking. Clerk: Now, don't worry, sir. Give me your luggage tags and we'll soon find them.

content.transcript: Girl: Excuse me, officer. Can you help me, please? My name is June and I've lost my sister, Kate. Officer: Oh, dear! How old is she? Girl: Ten. She's my twin sister. She's the same age as me. Officer: And does she look the same as you? Girl: No, not really. She's not as tall as me. And she's a little bit fatter. She eats a lot you see. Officer: Is her hair the same colours as yours? Girl: Yes, but mine isn't as long as hers. Hers is much longer. Officer: What is she wearing? Girl: The same as I am — except her T-shirt is red. Officer: And when did you last see her? Girl: Oh. About half an hour ago. Officer: All right. Don't worry. Come along with me and we'll soon find your sister. Girl: Ok. Thank you.

activities.title: Understanding Indirect Questions
activities.instruction: Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct option to learn about indirect questions.

options.feedback: This is a direct question. It's correct, but can sound less polite.

options.text: Can you tell me where the bookshop is?
options.feedback: Correct! This is an indirect question, which is a more polite way to ask.

questions.question: Which sentence is a more polite way to ask for information?
questions.explanation: We often use phrases like 'Can you tell me...' or 'Do you know...' to make questions more polite. These are called indirect questions.

options.feedback: Incorrect. In an indirect question, the word order is like a statement (subject + verb), not a question (verb + subject).
Excellent! The word order changes. 'What time is it?' (direct) becomes '...what time it is' (indirect).

questions.question: What is the correct word order for this indirect question: 'Do you know...'
questions.explanation: In an indirect question, the part after the question word (what, where, how) uses statement word order (subject before the verb), not question word order.

activities.title: Making Questions Polite
activities.instruction: Change the direct questions into polite, indirect questions using the phrase provided. This is the same as Workbook page 4, exercise C.
activities.compensates: Workbook activity 1.3C, providing instant feedback.

correct: Do you know where I can buy a spade?
sentences.original: Where can I buy a spade?
sentences.explanation: The word order in the main part of the question stays the same because 'can' is a modal verb.

correct: Can you tell me how far the bus station is?
sentences.original: How far is the bus station?
sentences.explanation: The verb 'is' moves to the end, after the subject 'the bus station'.

correct: Do you know what time the bookshop opens?
sentences.original: What time does the bookshop open?
sentences.explanation: We remove the auxiliary verb 'does' and add 's' to the main verb 'open'.

correct: Do you know what Faisal’s telephone number is?
sentences.original: What is Faisal’s telephone number?
sentences.explanation: The verb 'is' moves to the end, after the subject 'Faisal's telephone number'.

content.passage: To keep healthy, it is important to follow some basic rules. First, a balanced diet is essential. This means eating a variety of foods, including fruits which are full of vitamins, and avoiding too many fats. Second, regular exercise helps keep your body fit and strong. Third, good hygiene can prevent the spread of diseases. For example, cleaning a small injury with disinfectant can stop an infection from developing. For more serious illnesses like the flu, rest is important. Sometimes, a doctor might give you a prescription for tablets to help you recover. Finally, prevention is key. For diseases like cholera, it is crucial to be immunized, especially when traveling. Following this advice can help you avoid getting sick and needing a doctor.

content.transcript: Crossbreeding, or creating hybrid animals, is only possible when two animals are part of the same family. This is because their genetic makeup is similar enough to produce offspring. The liger, a mix of a male lion and a female tiger, is one famous example. Another is the cama, born from a male camel and a female llama. Scientists were interested in the cama because they hoped to combine the camel's size and strength with the llama's valuable wool coat. While these hybrids are fascinating, they often cannot reproduce themselves and usually live in captivity rather than in the wild.

activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the article from Pupil's Book page 3. Then, answer the multiple-choice questions to check your understanding.
activities.compensates: Digitizes the reading comprehension task from WB1.4A, providing instant feedback and varied question types.

content.passage:
Animals are divided into families. The house-cat is of the same family as its much bigger cousins, the lions of Africa and the tigers of India. The dog, the wolf and the jackal are part of the dog family. If animals are part of the same family, it is sometimes possible to crossbreed them to make a new animal. This was done several years ago when a lion was crossbred with a tiger, giving us a new animal called a ‘liger’. Now, it has been done again. The new animal is called a ‘cama’, and has been given the name Rama.

Rama the cama was born in Dubai in January, 1998. It is a cross between a male camel and a female llama. Although they are from the same family of animals, they are very different. Camels live mainly in hot countries like Arabia, whereas llamas live in mountainous parts of South America where it gets very, very cold. Because of the intense cold at heights of 4,000 metres, llamas have coats of long, heavy wool.

So what does Rama look like? Unlike its father, it has no hump on its back. Like its father, it has the short ears and the long tail of the camel. It is bigger than a llama but not as big as a camel. However, the wool coat of the llama, which is very valuable, unlike the hair coat of the camel, which has little value.

content.transcript: Many people debate whether city life is better than country life. The city is certainly more exciting than the countryside; however, it is also much noisier. In the city, you have many job opportunities. Unlike the countryside, where jobs can be limited, the city offers a wide range of careers. The cost of living is a major point of contrast. activities.title: Read the Story: Barry Jones - London schoolboy
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the story about Barry's bad morning. Then answer the questions to check your understanding.
activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led reading of PB page 6 and gist questions.

content.passage:
'Come on, Sue. Give me the cornflakes. I'm late.'
'Say please,' said Sue, giggling.
'Please,' I said. 'And hurry up! It's half past eight!'
'Dad can take you in his taxi,' said Sue.
'No, he can't. He's gone,' I said.
'Do you want an egg, dear?' shouted Mum from the kitchen.
'No thanks, Mum. I'm late.'
Sue giggled again and I wanted to know why.
'What are you laughing at?'
'Nothing,' said Sue and giggled for the third time.
Sue was just thirteen, about two years younger than me, and sometimes I could not understand her.

Ten minutes later, I was sitting upstairs on the bus with my Geography textbook open on my knee. There was a test in the first period.
'Hi, Barry,' somebody said behind me. It was my friend, Kevin. We had been at Central Comprehensive School for almost five years. I turned round and Kevin laughed. 'Your face!' he said. 'It's all black. Don't you wash?'
'Sue!' I shouted. She had put some trick soap in the bathroom before I went in. My face had got dirtier instead of cleaner.

The bus stopped. We flew downstairs and I ran to the school washroom. Then I ran to the Geography lesson.
'I'm sorry I'm late, sir,' I panted.
'I'm sorry too,' said Mr Edwards, our Geography teacher. 'Sit down and do the test.'

'Where's that soap, Sue?' I asked when I got home. She didn't answer.
'Anne's coming,' she said.
'Who's Anne?' I asked.
'She's my pen-friend from France,' said Sue. 'She's coming to stay next week - for a month.'

content.transcript: Welcome. Today we're looking at a classic landscape. In the distance, you can see a tall mountain range. From these mountains, a small stream begins its journey, growing into a wide river as it flows through the green valley below. The land in the valley is very fertile, so it's mostly used as farmland for growing crops. The river continues until it reaches the sea, creating a beautiful and varied coastline. On a sunny day, it's a perfect view. However, on a misty day, the mountains can disappear completely.

activities.title: Listening for Gist
activities.instruction: Listen carefully! 🎧 Clear your ears and to the conversation between Mike and Andy. Then, answer the questions about the general situation. This is based on WB Page 2, Exercise A.
activities.compensates: Replaces the teacher-led listening for gist activity (WB1.7A) where the teacher plays a cassette.

What time of day is it?
At the end of the conversation, how are Andy and Mike feeling?

content.transcript: Mike: Andy! Andy! Andy: Over here. Mike: There you are! I've been looking for you for hours! Are you Ok? Andy: Yes ... I'm fine. Mike: Are you hurt? Andy: I ... don't know. I'll try to get up. Aaah. No, I've hurt my leg. Mike: Here. Let me see. Mmm. I think it's broken. What happened? Andy: I was crossing the river when I slipped. I fell into the water and I must have hit my head on a rock, because I don't remember anything else until I heard you calling, just now. Mike: The river carried you miles. I'm surprised you didn't drown. Andy: I'm certainly very wet ... and very cold. Mike: Here, have my jacket. Andy: What time is it? Mike: Half past five. It's getting dark. We've got to get off this mountain before nightfall. Andy: So what are we going to do? You can't carry me down. Mike: That's true. You're too fat! Andy: Thanks a lot! Mike: I've got my mobile phone. I'll call for help. Andy: But ... do you know where we are? Mike: I think so. Let's look at the map. We came up this big valley together, and crossed the river once. Then we climbed this hill on the left - it's called High View - and you went on ahead towards Snow peak. Why didn't you wait for me? Andy: I wanted to see the view from the top. You were moaning about wanting to get back ... Mike: I was worried about the weather. Look, it's getting misty. It was sunny when we started ... Andy: Well, anyway. You must have fallen into this river here, on the west side of Snow peak. I waited for ages for you to come back, then I followed you up the top and saw the other river. I found your tracks on this side of the river, but nothing on the other side, so I followed the river down for about 5 kilometres. So I think we are about here, near Sheep Moor. Look! Those fields in the distance must be Cliff Farm. Andy: Ok. So call in the mountain rescue people. Mike: Right ... Oh, no! Andy: What? Mike: The battery on the phone's dead.

activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the text about a drive in the countryside. Then answer the questions that follow. This is based on the text from Pupil's Book page 6.
activities.compensates: Teacher-led reading of PB page 6 and comprehension questions from WB page 4, Activity B.

content.passage:
I decided to spend my holiday in Wales, and one day I went for a drive. I began on the main coast road. To my left, the sea stretched out to the horizon. In a large field, some cows were grazing peacefully. A bit closer to my car, a farmer on a red tractor was ploughing the newly-turned over soil, and a flock of birds followed him, looking for something to eat.

After a while, I turned off the coast road and headed inland. The road began to get higher and steeper. Soon, I could see a river in the valley below me. As I drove further up the mountain, the road became narrower, and the river also became narrower until it was just a small stream.

The road finally ended near the top of the hill. From there, I had to walk. The rocky peak was still high above me, but the view was already amazing. I could just make out the town where I was staying in the distance. After reaching the peak, I climbed down a little way because I was hungry and thirsty and wanted to eat my sandwiches.

The weather was hot and sunny as I started to eat. It was perfect. Suddenly, however, a cold mist rolled in from the sea. The clouds covered the sun, and it became quite cold. My perfect picnic was over!

lessons.title: Conditional Sentences
lessons.description: Practice Type 1 and Type 2 conditional sentences

activities.title: Conditional Sentences
activities.instruction: Learn about the two types of conditional sentences.

content.passage:
Type 1 Conditionals:
When a condition is likely to be fulfilled, the result is likely to happen.
Structure: If + present simple, ... will + verb
Example: If I work hard, I will pass the exam.

Type 2 Conditionals:
When a condition is not likely or impossible, the result is not likely to happen.
Structure: If + past simple, ... would + verb
Example: If I had a helicopter, I would fly over the mountains.

content.transcript: Abla: Hello, Muna? Muna: Hi Abla! How are you? Abla: I'm fine, thanks. Listen, is Shareefa there? Muna: No, she's not here right now. I'm just finishing my science project. I have to finish it before dinner. Abla: Oh, okay. Can you give her a message for me? Muna: Sure. What is it? Abla: Please tell her that the library trip is confirmed for tomorrow at 10 AM. She has to bring her library card. If she forgets it, she won't be able to borrow books. Muna: Okay, library trip at 10 AM, and she has to bring her card. Got it. I'll tell her as soon as she gets back. Abla: Thanks, Muna! Talk to you later. Muna: Bye!

activities.title: Grammar Rule: Present Tenses
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the examples and complete the rules about the present simple and present continuous tenses. This is from Workbook page 13, section A.

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: Example 1: Mr Al Sabri and his family live in Yemen. (This happens regularly).
Example 2: Now they are staying in London. (This is happening now).
Rule 1: The ___ tense is for things that are happening now.
sentences.explanation: We use the present continuous (am/is/are + verb-ing) for actions happening at the moment of speaking.

sentences.text: Rule 2: The ___ tense is for things that happen every day or are always true.
sentences.explanation: We use the present simple for routines, habits, and facts.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Tense
activities.instruction: Read each sentence and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct verb form: Present Simple for routines or Present Continuous for actions happening now.

options.feedback: We use the present continuous for actions happening now. 'Listen!' is a clue.
Correct! This is happening right now.
This is the wrong form for the plural subject 'birds'.

questions.question: Listen! The birds ___ in the garden.
questions.explanation: The word 'Listen!' indicates that the action is happening at this moment, so we use the present continuous tense.

options.feedback: This describes a routine, not something happening now.
Remember to add '-es' for he/she/it in the present simple.
Correct! 'Every day' tells us this is a routine.

questions.question: My father ___ to work by car every day.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'every day' signals a routine or habit, which requires the present simple tense.

options.feedback: The first part of the sentence suggests an action in progress.
Excellent! This is happening now.
This form is for he/she/it, not 'I'.

questions.question: Please be quiet. I ___ to study for my exam.
questions.explanation: The request 'Please be quiet' implies that the action of studying is happening at the moment of speaking.

options.feedback: Perfect! 'Usually' for the routine, and 'today' for the current action.
Check the time words. 'Usually' goes with present simple, and 'today' with present continuous.
The second action is happening today, which is different from the usual routine.

questions.question: We usually ___ football on Fridays, but today we ___ tennis.
questions.explanation: The first part describes a routine ('usually'), so it needs the present simple. The second part describes a specific action for 'today', so it needs the present continuous.

activities.title: Adding Emphasis
activities.instruction: Complete the sentences by repeating the comparative adjective or adverb to add emphasis.
activities.compensates: Provides focused, interactive practice on using repetition for emphasis, a specific stylistic device.

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: He drove ___ and ___.
sentences.explanation: We repeat the comparative 'faster' to emphasize the increasing speed.

sentences.text: I got ___ and ___ worried.
sentences.explanation: We repeat 'more' to emphasize the growing feeling of worry.

sentences.text: The music became ___ and ___.
sentences.explanation: Repeat the comparative 'louder' to show the volume was continuously increasing.

sentences.text: As the day went on, the weather got ___ and ___.
sentences.explanation: Repeat the irregular comparative 'worse' to emphasize the deteriorating weather.

activities.title: Shifting the Focus
activities.instruction: Rewrite the sentence to change the focus by moving the adverbial phrase to the beginning. Remember to invert the subject and the verb 'to be'.
activities.compensates: Provides interactive practice for sentence inversion, which is often a teacher-led drill or a static worksheet exercise.

sentences.original: There were lots of goats on top of the hill.
sentences.explanation: The adverbial phrase 'On top of the hill' is moved to the front, and the verb 'were' now comes before the subject 'lots of goats'.
sentences.correct_transformation: On top of the hill were lots of goats.

sentences.original: Some of the hills were to the right of the road.
sentences.explanation: The phrase 'To the right of the road' moves to the front for emphasis, and the verb 'were' is inverted with the subject 'some of the hills'.
sentences.correct_transformation: To the right of the road were some of the hills.

sentences.original: A small, wooden boat was in the middle of the lake.
sentences.explanation: To focus on the location, we move 'In the middle of the lake' to the start and invert the subject and verb.
sentences.correct_transformation: In the middle of the lake was a small, wooden boat.

sentences.original: An old castle stands on the highest mountain.
sentences.explanation: In this case, with a verb other than 'to be', the subject and verb can still be inverted for stylistic effect.
sentences.correct_transformation: On the highest mountain stands an old castle.

activities.title: Joining Sentences with '-ing'
activities.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one by using the '-ing' form of the verb in the second sentence.
activities.compensates: Replaces a traditional sentence-combining worksheet with an interactive format that provides immediate feedback.

sentences.original: The children ran out of school. They were laughing and shouting happily.
sentences.explanation: The second sentence describes an action happening at the same time as the first. We can join them using a present participle phrase.
sentences.correct_transformation: The children ran out of school, laughing and shouting happily.

sentences.original: The man sat by the window. He was reading a book.
sentences.explanation: Combine the sentences by changing 'He was reading' to the participle phrase 'reading a book'.
sentences.correct_transformation: The man sat by the window, reading a book.

sentences.original: She walked down the street. She was listening to music.
sentences.explanation: The action of listening happens at the same time as walking, so we can use an '-ing' clause.
sentences.correct_transformation: She walked down the street, listening to music.

sentences.original: The team celebrated their victory. They were singing their team song.
sentences.explanation: Change the second sentence to a participle phrase to describe how they celebrated.
sentences.correct_transformation: The team celebrated their victory, singing their team song.

activities.instruction: Word choice matters! ✍️ Use your eyes! 🧐 Look closely at the at the dialogue again. Which of these words best describes the fisherman's attitude toward his rescuers?
activities.compensates: Workbook exercise 1.14 (written answers) and class discussion.

options.text: I would take the matches away from her immediately.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the safest and most responsible action.

options.text: I would ask her to make a small fire.
options.feedback: This is very dangerous. You should never play with matches.

options.text: I would tell my parents later.
options.feedback: This is not fast enough. You need to act immediately to prevent an accident.

questions.question: What would you do if you saw your small sister playing with matches?
questions.explanation: In a dangerous situation, the best response is to stop the danger quickly and safely.

options.text: I would throw water on it.
options.feedback: Incorrect! Throwing water on an oil fire makes it much worse and can cause an explosion.

options.text: I would cover the pan with a lid or a wet cloth.
options.feedback: Correct! Covering the fire cuts off the oxygen and puts it out safely.

options.text: I would run out of the house.
options.feedback: While you should get to safety, the first step is to try to put out a small fire safely if you can.

questions.question: What would you do if you were cooking with oil and the oil caught fire?
questions.explanation: It's important to know the correct safety procedure for different types of fires. Never use water on an oil fire.

options.text: I would jump in the water to save them.
options.feedback: This can be very dangerous unless you are a trained lifeguard. The drowning person might pull you under.

options.text: I would shout for help and try to throw them something that floats.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the safest way to help. Get the attention of others and provide a flotation device.
You should always try to help in a safe way.

questions.question: What would you do if you saw somebody drowning?
questions.explanation: The safety rule is 'Reach, Throw, Row, Go'. Try to help from a safe distance before entering the water yourself.

activities.title: Reflexive Pronouns
activities.instruction: Learn the reflexive pronouns. These are used when the subject and the object of a verb are the same person or thing.
activities.compensates: Vocabulary presentation by the teacher.

cards.example: I can't lift this table by myself.
cards.definition: Used by a speaker to refer to himself or herself as the object of a verb or preposition.

cards.example: Don't swallow those pills! You'll poison yourself.
cards.definition: Used to refer to the person being addressed as the object of a verb or preposition (singular).

cards.example: He taught himself to play the guitar.
cards.definition: Used to refer to a male person as the object of a verb or preposition.

cards.example: Noura hurt herself when she fell down the stairs.
cards.definition: Used to refer to a female person as the object of a verb or preposition.

cards.example: The cat is washing itself.
cards.definition: Used to refer to a thing or animal as the object of a verb or preposition.

cards.example: We should be proud of ourselves for finishing the project.
cards.definition: Used by a speaker to refer to a group including himself or herself as the object of a verb or preposition.

cards.example: You can do these exercises by yourselves.
cards.definition: Used to refer to the people being addressed as the object of a verb or preposition (plural).

cards.example: The boys took sweaters to keep themselves warm.
cards.definition: Used to refer to a group of people, animals, or things as the object of a verb or preposition.

content.feedback: Well done! You have mastered these new words. 🏮

activities.title: Using Reflexive Pronouns
activities.instruction: Complete the sentences with the correct reflexive pronoun. This is based on Workbook page 12, exercise A.
activities.compensates: This activity replaces the written exercise WB 1.15A, providing instant feedback.

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: Don't swallow those pills! You'll poison ___ .
sentences.explanation: We use 'yourself' when the subject 'You' (singular) does an action to 'You'.

sentences.text: The boys took sweaters to the camp to keep ___ warm at night.
sentences.explanation: We use 'themselves' when the subject 'The boys' (they) does an action to 'they'.

sentences.text: I can't lift this table by ___ . Can you help me?
sentences.explanation: We use 'myself' when the subject 'I' does an action to 'I'.

sentences.text: Noura hurt ___ when she fell down the stairs.
sentences.explanation: We use 'herself' when the subject 'Noura' (she) does an action to 'she'.

sentences.text: Listen, everybody. You can do these exercises by ___ . You don't need my help.
sentences.explanation: We use 'yourselves' when the subject 'You' (plural) does an action to 'You'.

activities.title: What Would You Do?
activities.instruction: Read the situation and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct response using the second conditional (if + past simple, ...would + verb). This is based on Workbook page 12, exercise 1.14.
activities.compensates: This digitizes the oral practice from WB 1.14, providing structured choices and immediate feedback on the correct use of the second conditional.

options.text: I would take the matches away from her.
options.feedback: Correct! This uses the 'would + verb' structure for the second conditional.

options.text: I will take the matches away from her.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is the first conditional. We need the second conditional for hypothetical situations.

options.text: I take the matches away from her.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is the zero conditional. We need the second conditional for this hypothetical situation.

questions.question: What would you do if you saw your small sister playing with matches?
questions.explanation: The second conditional is used for unlikely or hypothetical situations. The structure is 'if + past simple, ... would + base verb'.

options.text: I would throw water on it.
options.feedback: This is very dangerous! Throwing water on an oil fire can make it explode.

options.text: I would cover the pan with a lid.
options.feedback: Excellent! Covering the pan removes the oxygen and puts out the fire safely.

options.text: I am covering the pan with a lid.
options.feedback: Incorrect verb tense. Remember the 'would + verb' structure for the result clause.

questions.question: What would you do if you were cooking with oil and the oil caught fire?
questions.explanation: In this hypothetical emergency, the safest action is to cover the pan to cut off oxygen. The correct grammatical structure is 'would cover'.

options.text: I would shout for help immediately.
options.feedback: Correct. This is a safe and helpful action, and it uses the correct conditional form.

options.text: I jump in the water to save them.
options.feedback: This can be very dangerous unless you are a trained lifeguard. Also, the grammar is incorrect for the second conditional.

options.text: I would have shouted for help.
options.feedback: This is the third conditional, used for past regrets. The question is about a present hypothetical situation.

questions.question: What would you do if you saw somebody drowning?
questions.explanation: The correct structure for this hypothetical situation is 'would shout'. Alerting others is the first and most important step.

activities.title: Tense Review: Build the Sentences
activities.instruction: Put the words in the correct order to make sentences using different tenses. This is based on Workbook page 12, exercise B.
activities.compensates: This activity helps practice the sentence structures from WB 1.15B in an interactive way, which is difficult to do with open-ended questions in a self-learning format.

sentences.instruction: Make a sentence in the Past Continuous tense.
Make a sentence about a future plan using 'going to'.
Make a sentence in the Future Continuous tense.
Make a sentence about a future action using 'will'.
Make a sentence about a future arrangement using the Present Continuous tense.

activities.title: Pronouncing Reflexive Pronouns
activities.instruction: Listen carefully! 🎧 Clear your ears and to the pronunciation of each reflexive pronoun. Notice that the stress is on the second syllable (-self or -selves). Then, record yourself saying the word.
activities.compensates: Provides guided pronunciation practice that is often done by the teacher in a classroom setting (choral drilling).

activities.title: Memory Game
activities.instruction: Use your eyes! 🧐 Look closely at the at the picture of the busy street for 30 seconds. Try to remember as many details as you can. Then, the picture will disappear and you will answer questions about it.
activities.compensates: This digitizes the 'Memory game' suggested in the Teacher Guide (page 47), allowing for individual practice of observation and recall skills.

sampleAnswers: The man in the blue shirt was talking on his phone.
There were three cars.
Yes, there was a litter bin near the bus stop.
The building on the left was yellow.
promptQuestions: What was the man in the blue shirt doing?
How many cars did you see?
Was there a litter bin in the picture?
What color was the building on the left?

activities.title: Listen and Write
activities.instruction: Listen carefully! 🎧 Clear your ears and to the sentences carefully and type what you hear. Pay attention to the verb tenses and reflexive pronouns.
activities.compensates: This is a digital version of a classic dictation exercise, allowing for self-paced practice and automatic correction of spelling and grammar.

sentences.expectedText: At this time last month, I was preparing for my exams.
Next year, I will be studying at the university.
He hurt himself while playing football.
If I had more time, I would learn a new language.

activities.title: Match Digits and Words
activities.instruction: Match the number digit on the left with its correct word on the right.
